title: Everybody's Scared

pages.text:
Saturday forty-six began with the smell of burnt toast, which I let happen.

For the first time, I did not rush to fan the smoke alarm. I did not make a face. I just stood in the doorway with my arms crossed and watched Dad.

He was on his chair, waving a dish towel at the ceiling with the frantic energy of a man trying to shoo a very aggressive bee. The kitchen was filling with grey haze.

"Max! Good morning! Did you know I'm reading a book about anti-gravity?" he shouted over the beeping.

I said nothing. I just watched his face.

"It's impossible to put down!"

The beeping stopped. The room went quiet except for the ticking of the clock in the hall.

Dad stood there, towel hanging from his hand. For one second, just one, his smile didn't come back. He looked tired. He looked at the calendar on the wall, the one with the red circle around Sunday, and his shoulders dropped. It was like watching a balloon leak air, slow and silent.

Then he blinked, straightened up, and grabbed the toaster.

"Oops," he said, cheerfully. "Charcoal."

I realized then that the puns weren't jokes. They were a shield. He used them to keep the silence away. And I realized something else, something that made my stomach do a flip. Dad had never lived anywhere but here, either.
pages.image: Dad in a fish apron stands on a chair in a smoke-filled kitchen, looking tired while holding a dish towel, staring at a calendar on the wall; grey smoke swirls around him.

pages.text:
By Saturday fifty-one, I had learned that Mom’s clipboard was not just a list; it was her lifeline.

She carried it to the fridge, the bathroom, and even the dog’s water bowl. With every click of her pen and sharp checkmark, she seemed to be trying to tick the entire world into order. I followed her into the pantry when she went hunting for canned soup. I stood behind her, watching the six stapled pages flip. On the fourth page, there was a small, tight crease that she kept adjusting with her thumb.

She turned to leave, but her hip checked the doorframe. The clipboard tilted.

I saw the folded paper.

The writing was shaky, different from her usual tidy capitals. It read: *Will the kids be okay? Will I be okay? Find the good pediatrician. Learn to make friends at forty-three.*

She straightened up and hid the page against her chest. Her eyes darted to me, then to the shelves, then to the fossilized french fry I was holding.

"I'm getting the soup," she said. Her voice was tight, like a guitar string tuned too high.

I didn’t say anything. I just handed her the fry. She took it, stared at it for a second, and put it in her pocket.
pages.image: Mom in the pantry, holding a clipboard to her chest with one hand, looking uncomfortable; Max stands behind her holding a fossilized french fry, looking solemn.

pages.text:
Saturday fifty-four was the garage fight.

It happened exactly as it always did, with Tessa slamming the door so hard the dust shook loose from the rafters like a sneeze. Usually, I would retreat to my room, put in my earbuds, and pretend the silence on the other side of the wall didn't exist.

This time, I sat down on the concrete floor.

I heard the drumsticks. *Tap. Tap. Tap.* A slow, angry rhythm against the metal door, then nothing. I pressed my ear to the wood and heard a small, broken sound underneath the quiet. It wasn't quite a sob, more like someone trying to keep their voice trapped in their throat and failing.

*Tap. Tap.*

"Go away," Tessa said. Her voice was thin and shaking.

I didn't move or knock. I just sat there, listening to my sister fall apart in a room full of empty boxes. I realized she wasn't angry at me; she was angry at the future, and the Kettle Drums, and the door to tenth grade that she didn't know how to open.

I stayed until her breathing slowed down, and the tapping started again, slower this time. I stayed until I couldn't stand it anymore.
pages.image: Max sitting on the garage floor, pressing his ear against the metal wall; through the wood, the faint silhouette of Tessa with headphones is visible, looking distressed.

pages.text:
Saturday fifty-eight, I went to the tent.

It was a fort built from moving blankets and broom handles, tucked into the corner of my room. Gus was inside, because he was always inside. It was his world, his safe place, the only part of the house that hadn't been packed into a box yet.

I climbed in. It was warm and smelled like green plastic and old carpet.

"What are you scared of?" I asked.

Gus didn't roar. He just sat there, knees pulled up to his chest, the spiky tail of his costume twitching against the blanket.

"Does the new house have a room for a T. rex?" he whispered.

I looked at him. He was six, wearing a dinosaur suit in ninety-degree heat, asking if his armor would still fit.

I looked down at my own hands. They were wrapped around my red hoodie, the one I wore every day even when it was too hot. I had been so busy trying to fix the day that I hadn't asked him if he was okay. I hadn't asked anyone.

"It does," I said. "It has a whole lot of them."

Gus nodded. He didn't look convinced. He looked like he was hoping I was lying, because a lie was better than the truth if the truth was that there was no room.
pages.image: Max and Gus inside a blanket fort; Gus in his green T. rex costume sits with knees up, looking worried; Max looks down at his own red hoodie, looking thoughtful.

pages.text:
Saturday sixty.

I lay on my air mattress in the dark, staring at the bare ceiling that had watched me fail for sixty Saturdays in a row. I had spent a hundred and twenty hours, or maybe a thousand, trying to repair the day. I fixed the toast. I saved the boxes. I memorized the puns and the worries and the secrets. But every morning, the clock would cuckoo, and the room would go back to being empty.

I realized I had been looking at the problem backwards. I thought I was the only one who was scared. I thought I was the only one who was losing something. But Dad was losing his friends. Mom was losing her life. Tessa was losing her band. Gus was losing his room.

I was the only one who remembered the loss. The rest of them just kept losing it, over and over, without ever knowing they were losing it. And I couldn't tell them.

I sat up, and the air mattress squeaked like a mouse in a sock drawer. So I did the only thing I could think of. I decided to fix them, too.
pages.image: Max sitting up on an air mattress in a dark room, looking determined and slightly sad; the bare ceiling is visible above him, emphasizing the emptiness of the space.
